question: What happened when QCOM breached $150.07 on November 20, 2026, and how do we resolve the Stage 1 vs. Stage 4 data split?

epigraph.quote: When price slices through structural support on heavy volume, respect the breakdown first and ask questions later.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein's Stage Analysis

web_blocks.html: On Friday, November 20, 2026, Qualcomm suffered a decisive technical breakdown [24]. Shares plunged -7.45% on the day to close at $149.94, down 15.00% on the week per TradingView (-13.06% in our 5-day facts ledger) and -42.31% below its $259.92 52-week high [24]. Volume spiked to 22.22 million shares (1.58x the 20-day average in our facts ledger; 22.28 million or 1.68x 30-day average in TradingView), confirming institutional distribution [24]. Most critically, the $149.94 close sliced through both Pivot S1 ($154.69) and our prior $150.07 structural invalidation stop [24].

web_blocks.title: Transparent Stage Reconciliation: Facts Ledger (Stage 1) vs. Snapshots Engine (STAGE_4)
paragraphs: Our quantitative market-facts ledger tags QCOM as Stage 1 (Basing) solely because the $149.94 close sits +0.18 ATR above its 63-day low ($148.25) [24].

However, our live snapshots engine classifies QCOM as STAGE_4 (AVOID_STAGE4_OR_BROKEN / CAP_REJECTED) because price trades -15.44% below a falling 50-day SMA ($177.31), -12.08% below the 200-day SMA ($170.55), and -18.68% below the 30-week SMA ($184.39) [24]. We adopt STAGE_4 for risk control.

web_blocks.takeaway: Every timeframe from 4-hour to weekly confirms Stage 4 distribution, while semiconductor breadth collapsed to 17% above 50-day EMAs inside a 10-distribution-day US Downtrend.

web_blocks.html: Notice how completely the market backdrop deteriorated in a single week [24]. Just seven days earlier, semiconductors outperformed the S&P 500 on healthy breadth; by November 20, only 26% of semiconductor peers sit above their 200-day EMA and just 17% sit above their 50-day EMA [24]. NVDA (-14.01%), TSM (-9.36%), AVGO (-12.19%), MRVL (-11.69%), TXN (-7.70%), and NXPI (-6.60%) all sit in Stage 4 alongside QCOM [24]. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 sits in an active Downtrend with 10 distribution days in 25 sessions and zero of nine sectors above their 20-day averages.

web_blocks.title: Options Desk Verdict: NO_OPTIONS_EDGE
paragraphs: Our options desk flags NO_OPTIONS_EDGE on QCOM: price ($149.94) sits below both the 50-day ($177.31) and 200-day/30-week ($170.55/$184.39) structural floors while fundamentals rate CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL.
We hold zero QCOM option contracts in the live options book, and high 6.23% daily ATR ($9.34) makes catching falling calls negative-expectancy until a multi-week Stage 1 base forms.

web_blocks.html: Why $149.94 Triggers Immediate Risk Discipline: With a 14-day ATR of $9.34 (6.23% daily range) and 4H RSI at 32.20 showing no turn, hoping for a bounce is dangerous [24]. Pivot S1 ($154.69) and the 200-day SMA ($170.55) now sit overhead as trapped supply [24]. The next chart shelf lies at Pivot S2 ($144.59), followed by the 52-week low at $121.99 [24]. Short interest remains modest at 2.72% of float, proving this drop is real institutional de-risking rather than a short squeeze [23].

What Re-Qualification Would Require: QCOM cannot leave CAP_REJECTED until three strict chart signals appear. First, selling must exhaust above Pivot S2 ($144.59) or the $136–$144 shelf and carve a multi-week Stage 1 base with contracting volume. Second, price must reclaim the 50-day SMA ($177.31) and close a week above the 30-week SMA ($184.39) on >1.2x volume. Third, the US market must exit its 10-distribution-day Downtrend via a confirmed follow-through day.

Why Pivot S2 ($144.59) Is Not a Green Light to Catch Falling Shares: When a stock falls -15.00% in TradingView (-13.06% in our 5-day facts ledger) and breaks its 200-day moving average ($170.55) by -12.08%, momentum traders often hunt for an automatic bounce at Pivot S2 ($144.59) [24]. Yet QCOM's 20-day Bollinger Band width widened to 24.77% while 4-hour RSI sits at 32.20 with zero bullish divergence [24]. Because the 63-day low at $148.25 sits right underneath Friday's $149.94 close, any weak open next week tests $144.59 immediately. In a Downtrend where zero of nine S&P 500 sectors hold above their 20-day SMAs, waiting for a confirmed Stage 1 floor saves capital from catching falling knives.

book_paragraphs: In Chapter 7, we saw that once you adjust for Qualcomm's flat share count, new $4.0 billion senior debt, AWS contra-revenue warrants, and $3.45 billion in stock-based pay, $149.94 offers zero real margin of safety. Now let us open the November 20, 2026 technical chart, because the tape just answered the valuation debate with an exclamation point.

On Friday, November 20, Qualcomm plunged 7.45 percent in a single session to close at $149.94, finishing the week down 15.00 percent on TradingView (-13.06 percent in our 5-day facts ledger) and 42.31 percent below its 52-week high of $259.92. Volume surged to 22.22 million shares—roughly 1.58 times the 20-day average and 1.68 times the 30-day average. More importantly, Friday's close broke two critical lines in the sand: Pivot S1 support at $154.69 and our prior structural invalidation stop at $150.07.

Before we go further, let us transparently reconcile a small split between our two automated data feeds. Our quantitative market-facts ledger still labels Qualcomm Stage 1 Basing because $149.94 happens to sit 0.18 ATR above its 63-day low of $148.25. However, our live TradingView and Stage 2 screening engine stamps STAGE_4, AVOID_STAGE4_OR_BROKEN, and CAP_REJECTED. Look at the moving averages and you will immediately see why Stage 4 is the honest call: Qualcomm trades 15.44 percent below a falling 50-day average ($177.31), 12.08 percent below its 200-day average ($170.55), and 18.68 percent below its 30-week average ($184.39).

Check all three timeframes together. On the weekly chart, RSI sits at 42.09 well below a declining 30-week average, with the 10-week EMA overhead at $169.00. On the daily chart, RSI has dropped to 35.10 and TradingView's composite technical rating reads Strong Sell at -0.56. On the four-hour intraday chart, RSI is 32.20 under a falling 20-EMA ($165.25) and 50-SMA ($170.99), with zero higher-low reversal turn in place. Every timeframe points down.

Even more telling is what happened to the surrounding market and semiconductor group. Just a week ago, semiconductor sector breadth provided a cushion. By November 20, the S&P 500 entered a confirmed Downtrend with 10 distribution days over the past 25 sessions and zero of nine sectors holding above their 20-day averages. Within semiconductors, only 26 percent of stocks remain above their 200-day EMA and just 17 percent hold above their 50-day EMA. Broadcom fell 12.2 percent, TSMC fell 9.4 percent, Marvell fell 11.7 percent, and NVIDIA fell 14.0 percent—all sitting in Stage 4.

Volatility has also widened. Qualcomm's 14-day Average True Range now stands at $9.34, representing 6.23 percent daily swings, while Bollinger Band width expanded to 24.77 percent. When a stock drops 7.45 percent on heavy volume through a structural stop while short interest sits at just 2.72 percent of float, it is not a short attack—it is genuine institutional liquidation. Trapped buyers now sit at every overhead shelf: $154.69, $169.00, $170.55, $177.31, and $184.39.

Our options desk matches that caution with a clear NO_OPTIONS_EDGE verdict. With price broken below both the 50-day and 200-day floors and business quality rated Cyclical Conditional, buying call spreads or LEAPS into a Stage 4 waterfall violates every risk rule. We hold zero QCOM options in the portfolio, and we deploy none today.

Where is the next real chart floor, and what would it take for Qualcomm to earn back Stage 2 consideration? Below $149.94, the next classical floor is Pivot S2 at $144.59, followed by the 52-week low down at $121.99. To ever qualify for new capital again, Qualcomm must stop making lower lows, carve out a quiet multi-week Stage 1 base with contracting volume, and then reclaim its 50-day ($177.31) and 30-week ($184.39) averages on expanding institutional demand alongside a healthier S&P 500 tape.

book_subsections.title: Deep Dive: Why Averaging Down Into a Stage 4 Breakdown Destroys Portfolio Capital
paragraphs: One of the hardest psychological lessons in investing is honoring a stop-loss order when it triggers by thirteen cents—$149.94 against $150.07—on a famous technology franchise. It is tempting to tell yourself that a one-day 7.45 percent drop is an overreaction, that RSI at 35.10 is almost oversold, and that holding for a reflex bounce will recover a few hundred dollars.

History shows why that rationalization is fatal to compounding. Stocks do not become cheap simply because they fall from $259.92 to $149.94, and oversold readings in Stage 4 regularly become far more oversold before a bottom forms. Look at what is sitting immediately above $149.94: Pivot S1 at $154.69, the 10-week EMA at $169.00, the 200-day SMA at $170.55, the 50-day SMA at $177.31, and the 30-week SMA at $184.39. Every single rally into those five overhead ceilings will meet trapped holders eager to sell at breakeven.

Even more important is portfolio context. As of November 20, the US portfolio carries a beta-weighted exposure of 233.5 percent with only $2,540.35 in cash—barely 3.38 percent of net worth—in the middle of a 10-distribution-day market Downtrend. Qualcomm alone carries an effective beta of 2.04. Selling into the stop breach raises $4,498.20 in cash, cuts high-beta semiconductor risk immediately, and moves us out of the path of Pivot S2 ($144.59) or the $115 Bear Case. We can always buy Qualcomm back months from now if it builds a Stage 1 base and reclaims Stage 2—we never need to ride a Stage 4 markdown down to find out where the floor is.

book_subsections.title: Multi-Timeframe Anatomy: Weekly, Daily, and 4-Hour Breakdown Signals
paragraphs: Walk down the three chart timeframes one by one so you can spot this exact Stage 4 signature in future holdings. Start with the weekly chart: Qualcomm sits at $149.94 against a declining 30-week simple moving average at $184.39, leaving price 18.68 percent beneath its long-term institutional trendline. Weekly RSI sits at 42.09, meaning weekly momentum still has plenty of room to fall before reaching classic washout levels below 30.

Next, examine the daily chart: Friday's -7.45 percent drop came on 22.22 million shares, or 1.58 times the 20-day average. Daily RSI dropped to 35.10, while the 20-day moving average ($169.85), 200-day moving average ($170.55), and 50-day moving average ($177.31) all sit far overhead. That alignment—short averages falling beneath long averages while price makes fresh lows on heavy volume—is the textbook definition of institutional distribution.

Finally, check the four-hour intraday chart: price sits beneath both its 20-period EMA ($165.25) and 50-period SMA ($170.99), with 4-hour RSI at 32.20 and zero higher-low reversal structure. Even if buyers step in briefly near Pivot S2 at $144.59, a single reflex bounce cannot repair five layers of overhead supply. Respect the multi-timeframe alignment, honor the $150.07 stop breach, and wait for a clean Stage 1 base.

Compare that chart against the rest of the semiconductor sector on November 20 to see why group sponsorship cannot rescue Qualcomm right now. Broadcom dropped 12.19 percent to $304.41, Marvell fell 11.69 percent to $122.28, NVIDIA lost 14.01 percent to $125.53, TSMC fell 9.36 percent to $319.14, Texas Instruments slid 7.70 percent to $263.75, and NXP declined 6.60 percent to $235.15. Every single one of those peers now sits in Stage 4 alongside Qualcomm, leaving just 17 percent of semiconductor stocks above their 50-day EMAs. When institutional money is actively selling the entire chip complex, individual turnaround stories almost never decouple upward on their own.

book_subsections.title: Pinning the Exact Reclaim Checklist Before Ever Returning to QCOM
paragraphs: Because good research builds institutional memory, write down the exact technical and liquidity footprints required before Qualcomm can ever leave Stage 4. First, price must stop setting lower weekly lows and build a multi-week Stage 1 base above Pivot S2 ($144.59) or the $136.00 to $144.59 shelf, with daily volume drying up on quiet pullbacks.

Second, price must punch cleanly back through the 50-day SMA ($177.31) and close a week above the 30-week SMA ($184.39) on at least 1.2 times average volume—more than 15 million shares on advancing sessions. Third, the 50-day and 10-week moving averages must flatten and turn higher beneath price, while daily and weekly RSI climb above 55 alongside a healthy S&P 500 market uptrend.

Fourth, check the four-hour chart and options desk before touching any leverage. A healthy Stage 2 breakout shows a clean higher-low base turn on the four-hour chart, narrowing Bollinger Band width instead of 24.8 percent panic expansion, and positive relative strength versus the S&P 500. Until all four signals appear together, staying completely out of Qualcomm shares and options protects your capital from further Stage 4 markdown.
